clue.text: Make hair curl, using roller, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to set hair in curves and ripples
second meaning: a roller is a long heavy breaker at sea, one example of this

explanation.surface: A hairdressing tip: curl your hair with a roller.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a hair roller; the second meaning is a rolling sea breaker, and 'perhaps' warns it is only one kind.
explanation.definitionFit: To wave hair is to put curls in it, and a roller is a large ocean wave, so one word covers both.

clue.text: Made a supreme effort and caught the up train

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the idiom for doing something lavishly or with great energy
second meaning: in Britain the up train is the one heading to the capital or a city

explanation.surface: Someone rushed and just managed to catch the train to London.
explanation.walkthrough: British railways call trains towards London 'up' trains, so taking one is literally going to town.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to town is an idiom for doing something with great enthusiasm or no expense spared.

clue.text: Cleric putting bomb on vehicle

indicators.note: putting one thing on another sets them side by side, the first ahead of the second

parts.note: the V-1 was the German flying bomb of the Second World War, written here as VI
a car is a motor vehicle

explanation.surface: A churchman is planting explosives on a vehicle, a terrorist scene.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, the first piece sits on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicar is a Church of England parish priest, a kind of cleric.

clue.text: Revised coach's list of educational establishments

indicators.note: something revised has been reworked and put into a new order

parts.note: the ten letters taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A sports coach has updated a list of schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholastic is the adjective for things belonging to schools and academic learning.

clue.text: Succeed with computer science? Don't be ridiculous

parts.note: a plan that comes off succeeds
IT stands for information technology

explanation.surface: A sceptic scoffs at the idea of getting rich through computer science.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal retort that dismisses something said as nonsense.

clue.text: Powerless pensioners — one's found refuge

indicators.note: powerless means lacking power, so the abbreviation for power is taken away

parts.note: OAPs are old-age pensioners
one is I, and 's is is

explanation.surface: Elderly people without electricity or influence: one has found a sanctuary.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the physics symbol for power; drop it from the old-age pensioners and add I + S.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is a fertile spot in a desert, and figuratively any place of shelter or relief.

clue.text: I have finished first, producing records

indicators.note: finished means coming at the end, so the words before it are placed last

parts.note: arch- as in archbishop means chief or first
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of winning a race and setting records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I have finished first' reads as a winner's boast; split it: I've comes last, and 'first' is a word for chief.
explanation.definitionFit: An archive is a collection of historical documents or records, or the store of them.

clue.text: Reproof evoked by misconduct ultimately given by leader in voice

parts.note: surface reading: a telling-off earned by bad behaviour

parts.words: ultimately given by leader in voice
parts.note: setter's reading: what the boss in the end delivers by speaking to the culprit

explanation.surface: A boss finally scolds an employee aloud for misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: No full wordplay could be found for this one: it reads as a description of a spoken scolding from someone in charge, and the answer was reached from that and the crossing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A talking-to is an informal word for a scolding or lecture, which is a reproof.

clue.text: Motorway menace often full of ice

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the plastic traffic marker lining roadworks
second meaning: the wafer holder for ice cream

explanation.walkthrough: 'Full of ice' suggests a frozen road; it is an ice cream in its wafer holder.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic cones line motorway roadworks to drivers' annoyance, and an ice-cream cone is a wafer filled with ice cream.

clue.text: It's not just the amusement park that's lost its head

indicators.note: losing its head means the opening letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a funfair is a travelling show with rides and stalls

explanation.surface: A complaint that a beheaded fairground is not simply a fairground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not just' seems to mean 'not only'; it means not fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Just as an adjective means fair and right, so not just is the opposite, unfair.

clue.text: Nicholas and Colin are sobriquets

parts.note: surface reading: two men's first names
setter's reading: Nick is short for Nicholas, and Colin began as a pet form of Nicolas, so both are names for a Nick

explanation.surface: A remark that two ordinary first names are really aliases.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as NICK NAMES: Colin is historically a diminutive of Nicolas, so both clue names are names for someone called Nick.
explanation.definitionFit: Sobriquets are informal or affectionate substitute names, which is exactly what nicknames are.

clue.text: Pass on cash

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to hand some money along to someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass on' reads as a phrasal verb, but it splits: the mountain pass, then the word on as it stands. The colón is the currency of Costa Rica.
explanation.definitionFit: The colón is a national currency unit, so it is a form of cash.

clue.text: Rent-a-party? It's a wind-up

parts.note: rent as the past participle of rend: ripped
taken as written
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A party hired out by the hour sounds like a practical joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like hiring, but here it means torn. The definition plays on wind-up as a tease: a tornado is wind that spirals upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air rising from the ground, punningly a wind going up.

clue.text: Jinn or gin?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a jinn is a supernatural being of Arabian lore
second meaning: gin is a distilled alcoholic drink

explanation.walkthrough: The near-identical sound of jinn and gin makes them look like alternatives; each is a separate meaning of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A jinn is a supernatural being, a ghostly entity, and gin is a strong distilled liquor; the one word names both.

clue.text: Point other people drew attention to earlier, long ago

indicators.note: to earlier tells you the words before it are placed ahead of the first one

parts.note: they means people other than ourselves
to give ear is to pay attention
a dot is a small point

explanation.surface: Others had pointed something out before, a long time back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drew attention to' looks like one phrase; split it so 'drew' links and 'to earlier' moves the pieces in front of the first one. The year dot is a British idiom for the very distant past.
explanation.definitionFit: Since the year dot is an informal phrase for an extremely long time ago.

clue.text: Powerful tractor, perhaps, one you can depend on

definitions.meaning: cryptic meaning: a tractor is something that tows, a 'tow-er', and a powerful one has plenty of strength
second meaning: the idiom for a reliable supporter

explanation.surface: Praise for a sturdy farm machine that never lets you down.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the first word of the answer as TOW-ER, a thing that tows, and a strong tractor fits it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A tower of strength is an idiom for a person who gives steady support in hard times.

clue.text: Somewhat imprecisely, these draw a dividing line

parts.note: surface reading: a loose way of putting things
setter's reading: high ground that separates the rivers draining one way from those draining the other, and loosely any turning point

explanation.surface: Things that mark a boundary, described with a hedge.
explanation.walkthrough: No wordplay was found: the clue reads as a hedged definition, 'somewhat imprecisely' since the word is also used for the basin a river drains and for a figurative turning point.
explanation.definitionFit: A watershed is a ridge of land separating river basins, and figuratively a point that divides two eras.

clue.text: Cutting a deep furrow, an industrious worker

parts.note: a trench is a long deep ditch
the ant is the proverbial hard worker

explanation.surface: A busy labourer ploughing a deep furrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' looks like the action of digging the furrow; it is the definition, meaning incisive.
explanation.definitionFit: Trenchant remarks are sharp and incisive, from an old word meaning able to slice, as cutting remarks are.

clue.text: Not christened or married? Only informally

definitions.meaning: cryptic meaning: christening and marriage are both ceremonies, so someone who has had neither has gone without one
second meaning: done casually, with no formality at all

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a couple skipped the church rituals and just lived together.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thinking of an unofficial relationship; the answer is a phrase for doing anything casually, taken literally as having no rite.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something without ceremony means doing it plainly and casually, with no formality, which is acting only informally.

clue.text: Oration delivered in one of the provinces

indicators.note: delivered means freed or set loose, so the letters are released into a new order

parts.note: the seven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A speech is given somewhere out in the regions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' belongs with the speech in the surface, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Ontario is a province of Canada, the most populous one.

clue.text: Duck has to fly

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to dodge or evade something
second meaning: to flee or get away

explanation.surface: A duck must take wing.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird that must fly is a decoy: both words are verbs about getting away.
explanation.definitionFit: To escape a duty is to dodge it, and to escape a place is to flee from it.

clue.text: Very dry — a litre could make you violent

parts.note: brut is the label for the driest champagne
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: A warning that a litre of dry wine might make you aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about drinking a litre and turning nasty; the letters come from the wine-label word for very dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutal describes savage, cruel force, a close synonym of violent.

clue.text: No-hoper getting nearer, but caught out

indicators.note: caught out says the cricket abbreviation for caught is taken away

parts.note: closer means nearer

explanation.surface: An outsider is closing in on the lead, but then gets caught.
explanation.walkthrough: C is the scorecard abbreviation for caught in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-hoper is someone with no chance of success, a born failure, which is what a loser is.

clue.text: Musician's patron spies insects crawling around inside

indicators.note: inside says one group of letters goes into the middle of the other

parts.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency

indicators.note: creatures crawling around turn back on themselves, so the word insects stands for is read backwards

parts.note: lice are small parasitic insects

explanation.surface: A musician's sponsor watches as insects crawl around within.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed insects go between the first and second letters of the spy agency: C + ECIL + IA.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Cecilia is the patron saint of music and musicians in Christian tradition.

clue.text: Vessel needing cover for interior

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a large passenger ship
second meaning: a layer fitted inside something, such as a bin bag or coat lining

explanation.surface: A ship whose interior needs covering.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocean liner is a passenger ship, and a liner is also a protective inner layer or lining.

clue.text: Group of schoolchildren construct accommodation for hare

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a class or year group in a British school
second meaning: the hollow where a hare lies

explanation.surface: A class of pupils builds a hutch for a hare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Construct' is itself a third meaning, the verb to form. In British schools a form is a class, as in sixth form.
explanation.definitionFit: A school form is a class of pupils, and a hare's form is the shallow nest where it rests.

clue.text: Different backing to the lady's

indicators.note: backing means moving in reverse, so the short word after it is read from its end

parts.note: taken as written
her is the possessive for a woman

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a woman's support takes a different form.
explanation.definitionFit: Other means not the same as one already mentioned, a direct synonym of different.

clue.text: Unusually, end phrase with a point

indicators.note: unusually tells you the letters appear in a way they normally would not, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to a writer to finish a sentence with a clinching argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With a point' looks like making an argument; it means having a sharp tip.
explanation.definitionFit: A pencil or blade that has been sharpened has been given a fine point.

clue.text: "A poor showing!" I cried to my converts

indicators.note: converts means changes into another form, so the letters before it are rebuilt

parts.note: the ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A missionary laments to his converts about a feeble turnout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My converts' reads as a preacher's flock; converts is the verb that rearranges the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mediocrity is the quality of being only average or second-rate, so a lacklustre performance.

clue.text: Run as a Communist

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to jog at a steady pace
second meaning: informal short form for a Trotskyist

explanation.surface: Someone stands for election on a Communist ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run as' suggests standing for office. The short word is also informal for a follower of Leon Trotsky.
explanation.definitionFit: To trot is to move at a jogging pace, and a Trot is slang for a Trotskyist, a kind of Communist.
